text:
I wouldn't buy a graphics card at these prices personally (got my GTX1660 for AU$380 which the exact same card costs over AU$700 now) but I do think this card is looking significantly better than the nvidia counterparts in terms of value in the current market, just based on my local retailers pricing (cheapest AU$ - only cards in stock):
RTX 3060 Ti: $1200
RTX 3060: $1200 (don't know why it's the same price as the Ti, both Gigabyte, but hey why not these days)
RTX 2060 Super: $1150
RTX 2060: $950
GTX 1660: $700

All while I can get a RX 6600 XT (several options in stock) from *$650*! I guess this is partially due to the demand of the Nvidia cards over this one (probably due to the bad rep this card is getting on the thumbnails of reviewers) but if you say it's competing with the 3060 Ti or on par with the 3060, I'd absolutely choose this card for half the price of those! 
Though that said, I still wouldn't spend over AU$400-500 on a new card, considering $300-400 got good low-mid-tier cards in the past (usually the GTX#60 cards or even the older 9800GTX+ when new)

text:
Here is a set of reasons IMHO why we are still excited about 1080p GPUs:

- as resolution increases linearly, rasterization time increases quadratically (we know how expensive 4k panels are, and how hard it is to drive them: the 4k crowd is still the minority, even the 1440p crowd; even we LTT viewers are a minority!)
- as the years progress, the compute power needed to render a frame gets higher as more effects are added in the name of "graphics fidelity"

Inb4 "this comment was made by the 1080p gang", I'm on a 5700 XT and a 1440p panel, and I'm trying to look at the market from the industry's perspective. This comment isn't about the pricing issue, which in a seller's market in the context of a silicon shortage (thanks governments' responses to the coof) isn't a surprise. This is about how the industry sees its market and develops what is cost-efficient in the "mid-range".

text: From my understanding the notion that most new games aren't already highly optimized is mostly false.  Modern compilers are actually quite good at compiling high level languages to machine code and even optimizing that code in various ways (high level vs low level coding is the main argument I usually see).  Modern game Engines are apparently a mixed bag with a decent amount of work needed to get the most out of them so that's one area where I could definitely see improvement.  Optimizing for newer components might not be the same as optimizing for older components which could also be something game devs work on since most new games are going to be optimized for the newest components.  Ironically Ray Tracing is something that could make optimizing games a lot easier in the future but at this point it requires newer hardware and is far from perfect.  I think the latest versions of DirectX and other graphics technologies are also designed to make optimizations easier but again, for newer hardware.

text:
MSRP GPUs are dead and have been for about a year now. It's better to say that MSRP everything involved in PC building is dead. Unfortunately the AIBs that try to stick to it are very few.  I was very  lucky to snag a RX6700xt a week ago at a reasonable price from an online retailer but i had to fork out a bit more than 2x the MSRP for it. A lot of people can't afford the kind of money that is asked for the new gen cards. Asking for 400 dollars for a 1080p GPU in this day and age is a punch in the gut and a stomp on the groin for a lot of people.

I managed to complete my PC build yesterday after i finally got my hands on my GPU. Build took 5 and a half months to assemble. Overall build cost me about 2200 euros (with a lot of stuff coming from other countries in the EU so shipping had to be calculated in that price). At 10% increase over MSRP this build should have cost me 1400 - 1500 euros (around 1650 with shipping calculated as well). Was this PC upgrade worth it? Yes it was and will be for a long time. Can most people build a similar PC?  Of course. If they can be patient and find parts that are reasonably priced like i did.

I got lucky while finding some parts while i had to completely drop my expectations about finding a GPU that was priced at most 2x the MSRP. For everything else i hunted down deals from overseas and prayed that my stuff would not be broken or lost during transit. GPU and monitor came from Germany. MoBo came from Greece. Ram kit came from Poland. Watercooler came from Austria. CPU came from Romania. Psu, case and other accessories came from my own country.

My advice to most people is this. Spread out your PC build. Hunt down deals from everywhere. It's even better if you live in the EU because, while prices may not differ much from retailer to retailer, availability is better from country to country. It will cost more than MSRP but if you spread out your purchases it will be doable. It's one thing to fork out 2.5k euro in a month but it's better to spread it over more months like i did. You will get your build. And when you do, it will be glorious. 

Patience young Padawan and all will work out.

text:
There's nothing wrong with telling people to go without.  It is a luxury item after all and not an essential.  I feel like most people (gamers?) are too emotional and can't do without this "want" of a hobby, which isn't surprising when we saw how successful loot boxes and micro transactions became despite how clearly low value and poor of a purchase they are.

I think a lot of people haven't considered what their ceiling is for this hobby.  I'm here with a 1080ti that I've wanted to replace with a 3080 but unwilling to pay much more than the MSRP of $700 for one, which is already a crazy amount.  At this rate, I'll likely never get to buy a 3080 since the shortage will be long term and these prices will likely hold indefinitely since the market has shown it's willing to accede to them.  At least MS and Sony have an incentive to hold MSRP since they make further money with royalties on games sold (where as AIB companies don't) but it can potentially spill over there too.  I've already decided that if that's the case, I'm just exiting the hobby.  I'm a fan and I enjoy it, but there is a limit.

text:
Here's my take: I don't NEED to upgrade but I would like to: I have spare money right now, my card is approaching 5 years old, my son is starting to get into gaming and needs a card to do stuff. I consider myself in a "treading water" situation. 

This card is highly attractive from a statistics stand point (rocking an RX 480 which is still a good card). BUT this price point is a big yikes. I can't understate that enough. 

$329 for a 3060 was going to be my jump on point but nearly 400 for a similar AMD card prices me right out. Since NOTHING is at MSRP right now, it doesn't really help until next gen cards are out and demand shifts away for this series. When that happens supply will still be low and won't increase because now everyone is building the new gen cards. This item is too little, too late.

Your review pretty much encapsulates how I feel so I can't really iterate more than what was already said. Thanks for trying to give honest reviews but as your team keeps saying: it's not a good time for PC gaming right now.

Just buy a high end card once and forget upgrading for 10 years, that is actually cheaper over time. 1 gen to the next doesn't make much difference anyway and won't anymore until something better replaces silicon after 2nm is used (cooling 350W with just air and 2 lbs of aluminum is already a monumental achievement, I don't ever see the power budget going over 500W without water loops being a requirement instead of a bragging right, heat pipes tend to "dry out" and quit working over that). If you already get 90-100 fps on a 27" 1080p screen from 2-3 feet you aren't going to notice a difference anyway without benchmarks. And pretty much every game developer designs games around the lowest common denominator of what people actually own, not the most powerful card currently made now or in the next 2 years, so no one actually needs the latest and greatest anyway since the average is still a 5yo card. text: @DerekDavis213  Believe it or not copper is a key commodity tied to the global  economy as much as oil. Recession = copper price falls. Boom = it increases. Reason is it's used in everything, not just circuit boards and wire but plumbing, roof flashing, etc. Still, you missed what I said in the previous post: raw material price used to make something does not matter much; time/effort/wages, R&D/warranty claims/taxes/long list of other overhead and built-in profit margins (without which essentially no one would bother making it at all, practically nothing is made by an NPO or charity) are around 75-98% (depending on widget and industry and market it's sold in) of just about all production costs. You really should take online economics 101 and business admin 101 courses, since clearly you currently don't have much of a clue of how those work in the real world. As far as video cards the main price increase culprits are tariffs (thank Trump and Biden too since he hasn't revoked that EO yet), and various BOM shortages (mostly silicon-based ones, not copper). When you can only make half of what you normally would sicne yteh parts are simply unavailable would then guess what? You will end up having to charge 2x as much to have the same income, otherwise a point comes where you won't make enough profit to stay in business without drastic downsizing. And sadly it's multiple issues compounding the upward price pressures, not just the BOM shortages alone (ie demand from crypto, working from home, people turning to retail site bots and scalping to eat and pay the rent after getting laid off from their hospitality job, etc).

text:
@Mr.Patchy  

1. Upgrading your computer is optional, but don't expect the same perfomance and resolutions you experienced in the beginning to translate into newer games. As time goes on, you'll have to tweak settings and possibly drop your resolution to accommodate for high frame rates. And that's not to say game optimization on PC is equal; going years with swapping parts will only have depending on devs to optimize their games while on console everyone has the same machine, so optimization is much more efficient, rather than assuming what the specs are recommended. So if you want to stay on the bleeding edge, or very close, out of necessity (for work) or higher fps at higher resolutions, you'll be upgrading every 2-3 years.

2. Consoles don't last for just only 7 years; they're completely operational til the day it dies. 7 years only applies to the window in-between release of the next console. Even when the newest console launches, Sony and Microsoft don't immediately drop support for the now last gen consoles; they know not everyone is going to immediately upgrade as the last gen library of games is massively huge and would take time. So those consoles would still get support well beyond their lifecycles with continued software updates and cross gen games for an extra 2-3 years. This is also when the now-last gen consoles are super cheap at retail and second hand markets; you'll already have a massive library of games to play until you decide to make the jump.

3. Steam sales aren't really an argument as you can get games relatively cheap on any platform aside from maybe Nintendo games. Physical games carry more value and can be sold second hand for not a lot of money. Sony and Microsoft now have more sales than they did in the past with games relatively new and old going for sometimes 60%-80% off in some cases.

4. While paying for online is dumb, it doesn't hurt my wallet at all nor likely anyone else's that really care about online multiplayer and cloud saves. You don't "need" PS Plus/Xbox Live/Nintendo online; some people a lot of people are perfectly fine playing single player games offline; that's what I mainly do on my PS5 when I'm not gaming on my PC. Not having those services won't brick the console. Even then, $60 a year for Plus and Live is nothing to most people; at least with Plus on the PS5, you get 20 free PS4 games with the addition of cloud saves and 2-3 games every month. Same can be said for Xbox. Nintendo's is well.... Nintendo. You realize there's far more egregious subscriptions right? Hell you don't even have to pay $60, you can do 1, 3, or even six months if you wanted to game online temporarily.

4. "You'll probably end up paying about the same or less for a PC as your console per year of use". Refer back to #2, #3, and #4. At the very worst, console would only be a slightly more expensive investment if you pay $60 every year (again, optional) and buy all your games at retail $60/$70 (in which most wait for sales anyway).

Side note: I play on console and mostly PC, so there's no bias nor fanboy nonsense.

I don't get it, 1080P max settings and high fps > 4K mid settings and same fps or max settings with either lower fps or higher cost.
Like 4K is unnecessary unless you have a bigger display further away anyway and it's not like the gameplay is any different in 4K, 1440P or 1080P regardless.
and for those who say 1080P looks bad, it will look worse on a monitor designed for 4K of the same size as a monitor designed for 1080P, the same as how older games designed for 1080P look sharp in even 720P while a modern game designed for 4K looks softer in 1080P and like hot garbage in 720P on a display of the same size.
I for one say get a high-end card and play at max settings in 1080P and it will last a lot longer than if you want to play in 4K, 8K etc. the GTX 1080Ti and even 980Ti can do 1080P no problem still and they're much older. but if you wanted 4K from them, the 1080Ti would be fine for a while longer, but the 980Ti would start to struggle.
I just believe that better lighting, shadows, hairworks etc. looks better than more pixels, because take a picture of some poop at 1080P and 4K, and the 4K image is still just a sharper image of the same pile of poop.

author: @tasneemkhandaker

text: @tasneemkhandaker  Enhanced Sync and Fast Sync solve tearing without adding input lag, but below the display refresh, Enhanced Sync acts like vsync off (with tearing) while Fast Sync acts like vsync on (with the terrible frame pacing) but with latency closer to vsync off. Neither are ideal solutions for low framerate gaming, as they are both designed for games to run above the display refresh rate, preferably multiple times faster. However, they're becoming less important with time, as variable refresh rate support is almost universal in new monitors these days. The cheapest gaming monitor with VRR on NewEgg is around $130, and while you can go a bit cheaper with non-gaming monitors, a 75Hz display with freesync is a big step up in fluidity and latency versus a 60Hz fixed refresh display.

text: The main issue is that GPU manufacturers saw their product's prices skyrocket due to Covid, chip shortages, and new tariffs. More importantly, they saw that PEOPLE WERE STILL WILLING TO BUY THEM EVEN WITH SKYROCKETING PRICES! Retail outlets like Newegg, BH Photo, Amazon, etc all sell their GPUs at drastically inflated prices or force people to buy them in bundles which increases the price even more. Naturally GPU manufacturers wanted in on the action, because all that extra profit being generated isn't flowing into THEIR pockets. That is why we're seeing 1080P cards for almost $400.

Look at where your current card sits; eg


Entry Level Gpu

Mid Range Gpu

High End Gpu

Enthusiast Gpu

However there is diffrent reason why that picture (although wrong in dimensions) is more practically correct. Imagine a giant wafer of 10000mm^2 having 10% error rate per 100^mm2. You can fit 42 smaller chips into it, and 9-10 on average will hit the bin. OR you can put 19 bigger chips, and average 10 will hit the bin. In smaller chip you can utilize wafer in 76%, in smaller chips you can only utilize 47% of wafer right. This is why smaller chips are quite easy to make. while giant chips like Nvidia A100 cost a fortune.

Now to have bigger effectivness from die, big companies test every die, and simply turn off some parts of die that do not work right, but not all parts of die can be turned off to make worse chip still usable, so smaller dies are still per mm^2 way cheaper to make.

text: @denvera1g1  I am so confused by your comments. First you try and make an argument that this gpu is "priced the same as 1080p cards 10 yrs ago", except it is $100 cheaper, performs much better and uses a fraction of the power and thus cooling needed. No trolling here, just your lack of comprehension on this product and similar products in it's price range.
author: @Ravenousjoe

text:
@Ravenousjoe  Last time i checked price isnt based on performance over previous generaton, its based on cost to consumer, and how much a company wants to put towards R&D for next gen divided by the expected volume
The 6600xt, 3060, 3060TI are all much less complex cards to build. Sure that small die might have cost just as much to produced as that full 100 die from 11 years ago, but thats still under $50 of the total value of the card. Everything else, the RAM, the VRM, the cooling, should all be cheaper except for the 3060TI the board itself should be less complex because they use physically fewer components
author: @denvera1g1

text: @denvera1g1  neat, except the fact that performance is the key metric that determines how much these cost. If you have a 6600XT that performs the exact same as a 5600XT for the exact price, than the product won't sell. The only reason why 30 and 6XXX series are selling so well is because of the shortage and high demand. Radeon and Nvidia are making record profits because they can somewhat justify the cost, and they are sandbagging on performance because they can.
author: @Ravenousjoe

text:
​ @Ravenousjoe Which is why i said 1080p cards have returned to their prices from 11 years ago. Yes 1080p games now require more power, but adjusting for inflation, the MSRP of the 6600xt/3060TI are the same as the GTX 570($420 adjusting for inflation)

 This performance per dollar price scaling  works at the top end halo products, but not for the mid range/low end where people just want to spend the same $250 for a 60 class card to play new games, at the same settings they have been playing with their old cards, now instead of $250 its $380-400 just a short 5 years later.
Sure, the 3060 TI is better than a 1060, but the games are also harder to run

text:
@Ravenousjoe  Great news for my argument that these cards are vastly overpriced. Sony recently confirmed that the PS5, which uses the same manufacturing node as the 6600xt, is selling for profit at its MSRP of $499. Now, Why does that help my argiment?
It helps because the PS5 has something more than just a GPU core and RAM. It has an 8 core processor a better GPU, built in networking, a high end SSD, a bluray drive, USB ports, and a power supply. Now that alone should put the price of the PS5 $300 above the lower performance 6600xt. But if we look at it another way, and adjust the PS5 to be comparable to the 6600xt, basing the price soley on die size and ignoring all the extra hardware you get with the PS5. If you were to shrink the PS5 die to the same size as ther 6600xt, and then shrink the price by the same ratio, the PS5 would be $384. JKust $4 more than the 6600xt but again, you get a high end SSD, power supply, disk drive, wifi, and LAN, as well as USB
